clue.text: How to raise one tempting subject of discussion?

definitions.text: How to raise one tempting subject of discussion

parts.words: How to raise one tempting subject of discussion
parts.note: the saying goes that if you mention the tempter he will appear, so naming him in conversation is the way to summon him

explanation.surface: Someone asks how to bring up an enticing topic in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise' reads as bringing up a topic, but here it means conjuring up: the one who tempts is Satan, and the proverb says speaking about him makes him turn up.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when a person who was just being discussed walks in, as if mentioning them summoned them.

clue.text: Dinner bill £10 — in hand £10.0.2d. What sport!

definitions.text: Dinner bill £10 — in hand £10.0.2d. What sport

parts.words: Dinner bill £10 — in hand £10.0.2d. What sport
parts.note: someone with a ten-pound bill hands over just twopence extra as a gratuity and then dashes off

explanation.walkthrough: Leaving 2d (two old pence) on a £10 bill is a stingy gratuity before bolting; the phrase is also a fast form of cricket where the batsman must run whenever the ball is hit.
explanation.definitionFit: The diner leaves a gratuity and flees, which is also the name of a quick backyard cricket game.

clue.text: Wise wearer of a runcible hat ?

explanation.walkthrough: In his self-portrait verse Edward Lear says 'He weareth a runcible hat'; split as LEAR + NED, Ned being any chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Wise means scholarly; Edward Lear wrote that he wore a runcible hat, so the wearer is Lear-Ned, the fellow Lear.

clue.text: But no help to a pop-singer whose disc has slipped ?

definitions.text: But no help to a pop-singer whose disc has slipped

parts.words: But no help to a pop-singer whose disc has slipped
parts.note: manipulating the spine treats a slipped spinal disc, but not a pop record sliding down the charts

explanation.walkthrough: 'Disc' is a pop record falling in the charts; the treatment that fixes a slipped disc in the back cannot help that.
explanation.definitionFit: This manipulative treatment of bones and joints is the usual remedy for a slipped spinal disc.

clue.text: See 1
A sleep-inducer

parts.note: one who puts subjects into a trance, from the Greek for sleep

explanation.definitionFit: Such a practitioner puts subjects into a trance-like state resembling slumber.

clue.text: Fishes, that tipple in the — " (Lovelace)

parts.note: a line from Richard Lovelace's 'To Althea, from Prison', with its last word missing

explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace wrote 'Fishes that tipple in the deep / Know no such liberty'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the poetic name for the sea, the ocean's depths.

clue.text: Knocking at the door, he is four up over the hill

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first part sits over the next
in a down clue, up means the words are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals
a tor is a rocky hill

explanation.surface: A caller at the door who is in his forties and past his prime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns IS + IV into VISI, and 'over' places it above TOR. 'Over the hill' reads as past it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone calling at a house knocks on the door as a guest.

clue.text: It's loaded !

parts.note: describes something weighed down with cargo

explanation.definitionFit: Something carrying a heavy burden is weighed down or burdened.

clue.text: Pre-fall excursion

explanation.definitionFit: A stumble comes just before a tumble, and a short journey for pleasure is an outing.

clue.text: Sprat dish

parts.note: the nursery rhyme says Jack Sprat and his wife between them licked the serving plate clean

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprat' looks like a small fish to be served, but it is Jack Sprat of the nursery rhyme, who could eat no fat while his wife could eat no lean.
explanation.definitionFit: A large flat serving plate is the dish the Sprats licked clean in the rhyme.

clue.text: "Was never face so—-my mind "

parts.note: a line from the Elizabethan song 'There is a lady sweet and kind', with the missing word to be filled in

explanation.walkthrough: The song runs 'There is a lady sweet and kind, / Was never face so pleased my mind'; the solver supplies the gap from memory.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the quoted line is filled by a verb meaning delighted or gratified, in its past tense.

clue.text: The silly fool finds no work outside in care of the military police

indicators.note: the words 'no work' are placed around the following phrase, so they sit outside it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
c/o, written CO, is the postal abbreviation for care of
MP is the abbreviation for military police
OP is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A dimwit fails to find a job and ends up in the custody of the redcaps.
explanation.walkthrough: NOOP (no + op) is split as N...OOP around INCOMP (in + c/o + MP).
explanation.definitionFit: A nincompoop is a foolish, stupid person, a simpleton.

clue.text: Knock some sense out of you ?

definitions.text: Knock some sense out of you

parts.words: Knock some sense out of you
parts.note: the idiom normally means to teach someone better, but read literally it means to knock you senseless

explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock some sense into you' is the usual idiom; here the blow takes your senses away, leaving you dazed.
explanation.definitionFit: To daze someone with a blow is to make them senseless for a moment.

clue.text: Eccentric men of letters ?.

parts.note: odd people are oddballs, and letters of the alphabet are written symbols

explanation.walkthrough: 'Men of letters' suggests writers, but it means the alphabet's symbols, which share their name with odd people.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddballs are called this, and so are the written symbols of an alphabet.

clue.text: Have another shot at document to save the shipwrecked Muscovite?

parts.note: a Russian, and in the Cold War a Red, a communist
a raft is what keeps castaways afloat after a wreck

explanation.surface: Someone is trying again at a document meant to rescue a Russian who was wrecked at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: To write a document again is to have another attempt at it.

clue.text: Old style cuppa and cards at the scene of the 1879 disaster

parts.note: tay is an old or dialect way of saying tea
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: Tea and a card game where a famous collapse took place.
explanation.walkthrough: The rail crossing over the Firth of Tay at Dundee in Scotland collapsed in a storm in December 1879, taking a train with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The rail crossing over the Scottish estuary collapsed under a train in a storm that December.

clue.text: How the meek succeed?

parts.note: the Beatitude promises that the meek shall come into possession of the earth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeed' looks like 'do well', but it means 'come into an inheritance', as in succeeding to a title; Matthew 5:5 says the meek shall inherit the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into property after someone else, as an heir does, is to succeed to it.

clue.text: It's Esther who confounded the scurrilous Greek

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A woman named Esther baffles an abusive Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Iliad Thersites is the foul-mouthed soldier who rails at Agamemnon.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's railing, insolent soldier at Troy is the classic abusive Greek.

clue.text: Like a century's last decade

parts.note: the 1890s are remembered as the '... Nineties' for their racy society

explanation.walkthrough: The 1890s in Britain were called the Naughty Nineties, a time of music halls and scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in the stock phrase for the 1890s means mischievous or improper.

clue.text: Supporter brought South of the border by James VI

definitions.text: Supporter brought South of the border by James VI

parts.words: Supporter brought South of the border by James VI
parts.note: heraldic supporters flank a shield; Scotland's royal arms used a mythical horned horse

explanation.walkthrough: When James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, the Scottish creature joined the English lion holding up the royal arms.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-horned beast is a heraldic supporter of the royal coat of arms, brought from the Scottish arms.

clue.text: Brute in disguise as a revolutionary ?

indicators.note: a thing in disguise has had its appearance changed, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A brutish man goes about disguised as a rebel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disguise' looks like the anagram signal; the 'in' is fodder, and 'disguise' alone rearranges BRUTEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotary engine's wheel spins round and round, so it is something that revolves.

clue.text: Segregate one so unpunctual

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
late means not on time

explanation.surface: Keep apart the person who is always tardy.
explanation.definitionFit: To set apart from others is to keep in quarantine or separate.

clue.text: Potato counter ?

explanation.definitionFit: A fried slice of potato and a small token used for betting at a gaming table share one short name.

clue.text: Material for a cuff ?

explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a piece of cloth, and also a blow with the hand.

clue.text: Being too wise too early would be highly esteemed, present company excepted

indicators.note: the company is present, that is, inside, the word for highly esteemed

parts.note: something precious is greatly valued

explanation.surface: A remark that a know-it-all child would be valued, apart from those present.
explanation.walkthrough: The stock phrase 'present company excepted' hides the device: 'present' puts CO inside PRECIOUS, and 'excepted' just completes the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A child developing knowledge or ability unusually early is said to be advanced for their age.

clue.text: Has this cat something of the ape in him ?

definitions.text: Has this cat something of the ape in him

parts.words: Has this cat something of the ape in him
parts.note: to ape is to imitate, and the imitating cat is the one who mimics others

explanation.walkthrough: A copycat imitates others, and to ape means to imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape is to imitate, and the word goes before 'cat' for a mimic.

clue.text: The priest has the remedy

explanation.definitionFit: A French parish priest is a curé, and a treatment that heals is the same word.

clue.text: Empty-headed and fat! That's saying a mouthful!

parts.note: O, a nought, means empty, and it goes at the head
rotund means round and plump

explanation.surface: Calling someone brainless and podgy is quite an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Orotund speech is full, round and pompous, the kind that fills the mouth.

clue.text: Like the producer's pet, to give a concrete example

definitions.text: Like the producer's pet, to give a concrete example

parts.words: Like the producer's pet, to give a concrete example
parts.note: a favourite actor is given the role before auditions, and concrete blocks are moulded before they reach the site

explanation.walkthrough: A theatre producer's favourite gets cast ahead of time; 'concrete' is the building material, poured into moulds before use.
explanation.definitionFit: Concrete made into shapes before being placed is moulded in advance, as a role given out early is assigned in advance.

clue.text: Gentle journalist applied for the contract

parts.note: tender means soft and kind
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A mild-mannered reporter bid for the job.
explanation.definitionFit: To put in a formal offer for a job of work is to bid for it.

clue.text: They quiver like birds

parts.note: as means in the manner of
pens are female swans

explanation.surface: Creatures that tremble the way birds do.
explanation.walkthrough: A pen is a female swan (the male is a cob).
explanation.definitionFit: These poplar trees are known for leaves that tremble in the lightest breeze.
